topics.title: Feature ladder on the shared 5-fold split: which known features actually move one LightGBM?
topics.body:
Many feature ideas have been shared in this competition (route keys on Flight Distance, original-data lookups, aux-task features, rating crosses...). I wanted to see how much each one adds on the same split, StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42), all with one LightGBM, adding blocks one at a time and checking the gain on each fold.

Ladder (OOF AUC, delta vs previous step, folds improved):
- raw 21 columns: 0.959089
- + route profile (per-Flight-Distance means of the other columns, count, residuals): 0.960333 (+0.00124, 5/5)
- + value counts: 0.960402 (+0.00007, 3/5)
- + fold-safe target encoding (FD, Age, FD x Class, ...): 0.960464 (+0.00006, 4/5)
- + original-data lookup + original-only teacher: 0.960941 (+0.00048, 5/5)
- + rating x context crosses: 0.960950 (+0.00001, 4/5)
- + aux-task block (33 cols): 0.961089 (+0.00014, 5/5)
- final: aux expected values only, crosses removed: 0.961174

A few things I didn't expect:
- Route profile and target encoding overlap a lot. Each adds about +0.0013 on its own over raw, but on top of the route profile TE adds only +0.00006. Dropping TE from the full set still costs -0.0003, though.
- Original data works as a lookup/teacher, not as extra rows. It stays clearly positive (5/5 folds) even after the route features.
- Rating x context crosses hurt this LightGBM on their own (-0.00048 vs raw, 0/5 folds), and removing them from the full set gained +0.00006. Others report they help CatBoost, which I haven't re-tested.

Caveats: these are fixed-round refit OOFs, with the round counts taken from early stopping on the same folds, so they are not an independent estimate. Deltas of a few 1e-5 are within the fold-to-fold spread.

The notebook rebuilds the final feature set end to end on Kaggle CPU in about 45 min (OOF 0.96110, public LB 0.96098). It writes id-keyed OOF and test predictions, so you can use it as a stacking member: https://www.kaggle.com/code/koumeimaki/s6e10-feature-ladder-what-helps-lightgbm

Credits for the ideas go to @goodpjw2008 (route profile, aux-task features), @evgendvorkin (original lookups/teacher), @busyaprime (route decomposition), @yekenot and @cdeotte. Happy to hear if anyone has measured these blocks differently, especially for CatBoost or NNs.

topics.title: Why seed-blend OOF gains don’t reach the LB: fold-averaging already took them
topics.body:
Twice this month a blend beat my best single model on OOF (+0.00014, +0.00018) and lost on the public LB. Public-LB noise was too small to explain it (paired sd ≈ 0.00007 at 60k rows), so I measured another cause on a held-out 20% “fake test”, three splits:

blend vs its better member | OOF | test, 5-fold average
two LightGBMs, different seed | +0.00023 | +0.00005
LightGBM + XGBoost | +0.00030 | +0.00011

An OOF row is scored by one fold model; a test row by the average of five. Seed diversity is the variance reduction that averaging already gives, so it shows on OOF and mostly disappears on test. Family diversity survives in part. This is also why 10-fold members help a stack for real (more data per model), while extra seeds of the same member mostly don’t.

Notebook with the code: https://www.kaggle.com/code/senanuretin/s6e10-why-your-oof-blend-gain-vanishes-on-test.

topics.title: 39 Simple Crosses That Help CatBoost
topics.body:
A specific feature group gave me a consistent improvement in CatBoost: **cross each of the 13 service ratings with `Class`, `Type of Travel`, and `Customer Type`**.

These **39 categorical features** improved all five validation folds in two paired experiments. Raising the training cap from 3,000 to 6,000 iterations preserved the improvement.

This is a measured result for a specific configuration. Categorical interactions themselves are already public ideas.

## 1. What changed?

The control model already includes:

- Four passenger categorical features.
- All 13 service ratings treated as categorical values, preserving zero as its own level.
- Four numerical features retained as numbers **and** copied into exact-value categorical columns:
  - `Age`
  - `Flight Distance`
  - `Departure Delay in Minutes`
  - `Arrival Delay in Minutes`

The candidate adds:

```text
Every service rating × Class
Every service rating × Type of Travel
Every service rating × Customer Type
```

For example:

```text
Online boarding = 2 | Type of Travel = Business travel
Inflight wifi service = 0 | Class = Eco
Seat comfort = 4 | Customer Type = Loyal Customer
```

| Feature view | Total features | Categorical features |
|---|---:|---:|
| Control: categorical ratings + numerical category copies | 25 | 21 |
| Control + 39 rating–context crosses | 64 | 60 |

No original-data rows, teacher predictions, manual target encodings, or public predictions are added. Both models use CatBoost’s native categorical processing.

## 2. Pseudocode

The rating list contains all 13 service-rating columns.

```python
PASSENGER_CATEGORIES = [
    "Gender",
    "Customer Type",
    "Type of Travel",
    "Class",
]

BACKGROUND = [
    "Class",
    "Type of Travel",
    "Customer Type",
]

NUMERIC = [
    "Age",
    "Flight Distance",
    "Departure Delay in Minutes",
    "Arrival Delay in Minutes",
]

def category_string(series):
    return (
        series.astype("string")
        .fillna("__MISSING__")
        .astype(str)
    )

def make_features(frame, ratings, add_crosses):
    # frame contains predictors only: exclude id and satisfaction
    X = frame.copy()
    categorical = PASSENGER_CATEGORIES + ratings

    for column in categorical:
        X[column] = category_string(frame[column])

    # Keep numerical values and add categorical copies.
    for column in NUMERIC:
        name = column + "__category"
        X[name] = category_string(frame[column])
        categorical.append(name)

    if add_crosses:
        for rating in ratings:
            for background in BACKGROUND:
                name = rating + "__X__" + background
                X[name] = X[rating] + "|" + X[background]
                categorical.append(name)

    return X, categorical
```

For each frozen validation fold, train the control and candidate with identical parameters:

```python
folds = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=42,
)

for train_idx, valid_idx in folds.split(features, target):
    for add_crosses in [False, True]:
        X, categorical = make_features(
            features,
            ratings=RATINGS,
            add_crosses=add_crosses,
        )

        model = CatBoostClassifier(**same_parameters)

        model.fit(
            X.iloc[train_idx],
            target.iloc[train_idx],
            cat_features=categorical,
            eval_set=(
                X.iloc[valid_idx],
                target.iloc[valid_idx],
            ),
            use_best_model=True,
        )

        # Save validation probabilities at valid_idx.
        # Average test probabilities from the five fold models.
```

## 3. Why might this help?

An explicit categorical cross represents a rating level within a passenger background:

\[
z_{r,c}(x)=\operatorname{category}\big(r(x),c(x)\big).
\]

For example, the model can distinguish an online-boarding rating of `2` from a business traveller from the same rating from a personal traveller.

CatBoost can learn interactions from the original inputs, but these columns expose selected combinations directly to its categorical processing.

That is a modeling rationale, **not a demonstrated causal explanation** for the improvement.

## 4. Experimental setup

Both experiments use all **699,635 synthetic training rows** and the same five folds.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Validation | Stratified five-fold CV |
| Fold seed | 42 |
| Model | GPU CatBoost |
| Depth | 6 |
| Learning rate | 0.05 |
| L2 leaf regularization | 3 |
| Model seed | 42 |
| Training loss | Logloss |
| Validation metric | ROC AUC |
| Early-stopping patience | 100 |
| Maximum iterations | 3,000 or 6,000 |

Within each experiment, only the 39-feature group changes.

## 5. Results

### Full OOF ROC AUC

| Maximum iterations | Control | +39 crosses | Δ OOF AUC | Positive folds |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 3,000 | 0.960486195 | 0.960822718 | **+0.000336522** | **5/5** |
| 6,000 | 0.960514870 | 0.960799268 | **+0.000284399** | **5/5** |

The result persisted after increasing the training budget. In the 6,000-iteration experiment, neither feature view reached the cap: all selected best tree counts were below 4,100.

### Per-fold ROC AUC

| Fold | 3,000: control | 3,000: +crosses | Δ AUC | 6,000: control | 6,000: +crosses | Δ AUC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0.960756 | 0.961012 | +0.000256 | 0.960847 | 0.960977 | +0.000130 |
| 1 | 0.959404 | 0.959724 | +0.000320 | 0.959459 | 0.959754 | +0.000295 |
| 2 | 0.961117 | 0.961485 | +0.000368 | 0.961125 | 0.961390 | +0.000265 |
| 3 | 0.960543 | 0.960992 | +0.000449 | 0.960538 | 0.960952 | +0.000414 |
| 4 | 0.960649 | 0.960937 | +0.000288 | 0.960645 | 0.960964 | +0.000319 |

Pooled OOF AUC is calculated across all held-out rows. Its change therefore does not have to equal the arithmetic mean of the five fold changes.

## 6. An unfavorable comparison: rating–rating crosses

I also tested four categorical rating–rating crosses against the same control at the 3,000-iteration cap:

- Wi-Fi × Online boarding
- Ease of Online booking × Online boarding
- Inflight entertainment × Seat comfort
- On-board service × Baggage handling

| Feature group | OOF AUC | Δ versus control | Positive folds |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Control | 0.960486195 | — | — |
| Four rating–rating crosses | 0.960511049 | +0.000024854 | 3/5 |
| 39 rating–context crosses | 0.960822718 | +0.000336522 | 5/5 |

The rating–rating group had mixed fold results:

| Fold | Rating–rating Δ AUC |
|---|---:|
| 0 | −0.000025557 |
| 1 | +0.000005498 |
| 2 | +0.000158354 |
| 3 | +0.000146670 |
| 4 | −0.000163339 |

I would not treat that tiny pooled improvement as a consistent gain. These results support testing specific combinations rather than assuming that adding more categorical crosses will help.

## 7. Public code and related work

The selected training recipe is available here:

**[S6E10 | CatBoost Rating Crosses | CV 0.96080](https://www.kaggle.com/code/wangxintong111/s6e10-catboost-rating-crosses-cv-0-96080)**

It requires only the competition data and writes:

- Full OOF predictions with IDs and fold assignments.
- Test predictions.
- Fold metrics and best iterations.
- Feature provenance and data hashes.
- `submission.csv`.

Related public work already discusses these underlying ideas:

- [Service-ratings discussion](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/playground-series-s6e10/discussion/744890): service interactions and passenger context.
- [Do Service Ratings Mean the Same to Everyone](https://www.kaggle.com/code/liamob96/s6e10-do-service-ratings-mean-the-same-to-everyone): two service-rating × travel-purpose interactions.
- [CatBoost CTR + GLM-Margin XGB](https://www.kaggle.com/code/goodpjw2008/s6e10-catboost-ctr-glm-margin-xgb-lb-0-96127): categorical numerical copies and categorical ratings.

comments.body: Independent confirmation: I added your 39 rating × (Class / Type of Travel / Customer Type) crosses to a CatBoost that already had route profile, original-data teacher and expected-rating features. OOF went 0.96109 → 0.96122 (5 folds) and 0.96137 with 10 folds, my best single model. So the gain holds on top of a much richer feature set, not only on a plain baseline. Thanks for sharing it.

topics.title: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) - Intro, Dataset, and Starter!
topics.body:
Hi everyone, I want to share a **secret weapon** for tabular data problems. There exists pretrained backbones that already know how to predict tabular data **without** requiring any work from us. We **don't** need to engineer features, we **don't** need to tune hyperparameters, we **don't** need to train a model. 🎉

With **Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs)**, we just predict the labels of test data! Its so easy and so powerful! There is nothing for us to do! 🎉

# Frontier TFMs
TFMs have improved greatly in the past few months (official TabArena leaderboard [here][7]). The models below are the current SOTA and they are achieving these CV scores using `train.csv` as is with **no feature engineering** and **no training**. That is amazing. These scores are beating GBDTs and MLPs that require hyperparameter tuning and feature engineering! (official TabArena leaderboard [here][7])

Below shows the performance of TFMs on our current October Kaggle Playground competition data (with statistics from running on 1xA100 GPU offline):

| Model | Precision | **OOF AUC** | Fit h (5 folds) | Predict h (5 folds) | Total GPU h | Peak GB |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| tabpfn35 | amp | **0.961145** | 2.45 | 1.86 | 4.31 | 19.9 |
| kumolarge | fp16 | **0.960036** | 2.26 | 1.83 | 4.09 | 23.2 |
| **XGBoost (tuned)** | **BASELINE** | 0.959852 | 0.11 | 0.00 | 0.11 | 0.2 |
| **RealMLP (tuned)** | **BASELINE** | 0.959311 | 4.43 | 0.02 | 4.45 | 1.9 |
| tabfm | bf16 | **0.958871** | 0.03 | 7.46 | 7.49 | 45.2 |
| exaone | fp16 (exaone default) | **0.958557** | 0.00 | 10.71 | 10.71 | 75.0 |
| kumosmall | fp16 | **0.958484** | 0.54 | 0.46 | 1.00 | 25.1 |
| limix2 | fp16 autocast (limix default) | **0.958474** | 0.01 | 22.82 | 22.83 | 64.0 |
| causilo | fp16 (causilo policy) | **0.958275** | 0.04 | 0.91 | 0.95 | 31.1 |
| tabicl2 | fp16 autocast, column embedding fp32 | **0.958088** | 0.03 | 1.14 | 1.17 | 83.6 |
| mitra2 | fp16 autocast, logits fp32 | **0.957075** | 0.00 | 20.14 | 20.14 | 54.4 |

# Configuration
To provide the fair comparison above, each TFM uses `n_estimators=8`, `full context`, and `mixed precision`. So Opus5.5 had to rewrite many of the TFM libraries. Pilots were ran first to guarantee that code changes match the model's original accuracy. Also Opus5.5 added saving KV cache in each case to make inference very fast.

# Baselines - XGB and RealMLP 
We observe that **TabPFN3.5** and **Kumo-Tabular large** both beat XGBoost and RealMLP! This is amazing. The XGB and RealMLP have their hyperparameters optimized and use only the 21 raw features. They also use `n_estimators=8` similar to TFM.

# Kaggle Dataset
I publish a Kaggle dataset [here][1] with each of these TFM's OOF and Test PREDS. They were inferred offline using `StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)` on my local A100 GPU.

# Starter Notebooks
I publish a Kaggle starter notebook [here][2] demonstrating how to infer [**NVIDIA's Kumo-Tabular**][4] on this month's October playground competition data. And @philippsinger published a starter notebook [here][3] demonstrating how to infer [Prior Labs' TabPFN][5] on July playground competition data.

I publish an ensemble of TFMs with public OOFs [here][6] demonstrating how TFMs improve the current best public ensemble from **LB 0.96167 => LB 0.96176**! 🔥 When looking at model importance, we see that 5 of the top 20 (out of 135) models are TFMs!

# Next Steps
Even though feature engineering and finetuning are **not required** as seen by the great results above. We can experiment with adding some features to see if it helps improve CV LB of individual models and/or stacks. Also we can consider finetuning these models on train.csv data too.

When using Kaggle's GPUs, I suggest using only a few `n_estimators` (like 2) and reduced context (like 25k to 100k) for speed. When running offline with better GPU, then consider using more `n_estimators` and full context (i.e. 560k per fold) like the table above shows and the dataset's OOF are. For ensemble diversity, we still gain a lot using Kaggle GPUs and reductions.

# Enjoy!

[1]: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/cdeotte/s6e10-tfm-oof-and-test-predictions
[2]: https://www.kaggle.com/code/cdeotte/kumo-tabular-starter
[3]: https://www.kaggle.com/code/philippsinger/tabpfn-3-starter-playground-series-s6e7
[4]: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Tabular
[5]: https://priorlabs.ai/tabpfn-3-5
[6]: https://www.kaggle.com/code/cdeotte/stacking-tfms-with-public-oof
[7]: https://huggingface.co/spaces/TabArena/leaderboard
